grid.cell_id: row * 720 + col, where col = floor((lon + 180) / 0.5), row = floor((90 - lat) / 0.5)
grid.cell_size: 0.5 deg is ~55.6 km north-south but ~55.6*cos(lat) km east-west (about 56 x 12 km at 77.5 S); cells are not squares away from the equator
grid.area_weighting: cos(lat) of the cell centre; used for every land fraction, Earth percentile/median, P0.5/P99.5 clip, top-x% threshold and validation percentile
grid.distance: great-circle (haversine) with body radius (Earth 6371.0088 km = IUGG mean radius, canonical; Moon 1737.4 km, Mars 3396.19 km)

factors.name: Mean surface temperature

layers.moon: Diviner GCP 0.5 deg Tbol mean over local time (grid); polar targets: Diviner Polar Resource Product (south) annual temp_avg, mean of ~470 m triangles in the target window
layers.mars: Mars Climate Database v6.2 tsurf, mean over Ls x local time

factors.ui_copy: The average temperature of the ground over a full day and year. Cold limits how batteries, rovers and people work, and it controls whether water stays frozen. The Moon's shadowed polar craters are far colder than anywhere on Earth, so we match as closely as Earth allows and show what's left over.

factors.name: Diurnal temperature amplitude

layers.earth: NASA POWER hourly-LST skin temperature climatology TS_00/05/06/13/14 (2001-2020): mean over months of (max_h - min_h). Not TS_MAX(ANN) - TS_MIN(ANN), whose ANN values are the extreme months
layers.moon: Diviner GCP max - min over local time
layers.mars: MCD tsurf max - min over local time

factors.ui_copy: How much the ground heats up and cools down between day and night. Big swings stress materials, seals and electronics. The Moon's equator swings by roughly 300 °C, which no place on Earth comes close to. Mars swings less, and some Earth deserts get closer to it.

factors.name: Regolith thermophysics (thermal inertia class)
factors.units: class 1-5 (1 dusty, 2 fine, 3 sandy, 4 blocky, 5 rocky)

layers.earth: Apparent thermal inertia ATI = (1 - albedo) / dT (Price 1977), within-Earth percentile classes
layers.moon: Diviner rock abundance + regolith temperature anomaly, within-Moon percentile classes
layers.mars: TES thermal inertia 2007 (Putzig & Mellon), within-Mars percentile classes

factors.note: Never pool raw units across bodies; only within-body classes are compared.
factors.ui_copy: How quickly the surface heats and cools, which tells us whether the ground is fine dust, sand, gravel or solid rock. That matters for safe landing, for driving rovers and for digging. Earth uses a different measurement method, so we compare each site's *rank* within its own world, not raw numbers.

factors.name: Slope / landability
factors.units: fraction of area with slope < 5 deg

layers.earth: Copernicus GLO-90 overview reads (~360 m baseline); fallback ETOPO 2022 1 arc-min
layers.moon: LOLA LDSM_16 (global); PGDA 90 / polar 240 m for targets

factors.note: Slope baseline is recorded per body in provenance.json.
factors.ui_copy: The share of the area flat enough for a lander to set down safely. NASA's lunar lander requirement is a tilt of 8° or less, with 5° as the goal. Steep, broken ground is risky for landers, rovers and walking astronauts.

factors.name: Local relief
factors.units: m (P95 - P5 elevation over ~30 km windows)

layers.earth: ETOPO 2022 60 arc-sec; mean of P95-P5 over the four 0.25 deg sub-blocks of the cell
layers.moon: LOLA LDEM_16; targets from polar DEM, P95-P5 within a 15 km radius
layers.mars: MOLA MEGDR meg016; targets P95-P5 within a 15 km radius

factors.ui_copy: How much the ground rises and falls nearby, such as ridges, crater rims and valleys. Relief shapes shadows, line of sight for radios, and how hard a site is to traverse. We compare relief rather than altitude, because "sea level" means nothing on the Moon or Mars.

factors.name: Lithology

layers.moon: Unified Geologic Map of the Moon 1:5M rasterized + Lunar Prospector GRS FeO
layers.mars: USGS SIM 3292 rasterized + Mars Odyssey GRS

factors.ui_copy: The main kind of rock at the surface, for example dark volcanic basalt or the pale anorthosite of the lunar highlands. Matching rock type lets geologists rehearse sampling and lets engineers test drills and tools on realistic material. Lunar-highland rock is rare on Earth, so expect fewer good matches here for Moon targets.

factors.name: Aridity

layers.earth: Global Aridity Index v3.1 (Zomer et al. 2022, CC BY 4.0); Antarctica (not covered) filled with AI = 0.03 (hyper-arid polar desert, documented assumption)

factors.ui_copy: How little water the land receives compared with how much the air could evaporate. The Moon and Mars are bone-dry at the surface, so the driest deserts on Earth, such as the Atacama, are the best stand-ins. Dryness matters for testing life-detection instruments and for how soil behaves.

factors.name: Barrenness

layers.earth: ESA WorldCover 2021 bare/sparse + snow/ice fraction (CC BY 4.0)

factors.ui_copy: How much of the land is bare rock, sand, snow or ice instead of plants, crops or buildings. A lifeless-looking surface is closer to the Moon and Mars, and it keeps vegetation from confusing tests of cameras, spectrometers and robots.

factors.name: Ground ice / cold-trap access

layers.earth: ESA CCI Permafrost v5.0 PFR area fraction (2019-2023 mean); where CCI has no value (25N-60S band, ice sheets): 1 if POWER mean annual TS < 273.15 K else 0
layers.moon: min(1, PSR area fraction in target window / 0.10), raised to >= Ice Favorability Index (0-1 rescaled)
layers.mars: SWIM v4 depth band: 0-1 m -> 1.0, 1-5 m -> 0.67, >5 m -> 0.33, none -> 0; fallback Odyssey GRS WEH

factors.ui_copy: Whether water ice is likely just below the surface, as in permanently frozen ground on Earth or shadowed "cold traps" on the Moon. Ice is the key resource for drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel. Arctic and Antarctic permafrost lets teams practise finding and extracting it.

factors.name: Illumination regime (sun elevation)
factors.units: deg (median local-noon solar elevation over a year)

layers.earth: Analytic solar geometry (daily noon elevation, median over 365 days); POWER SW down as secondary
layers.moon: Analytic (obliquity 1.54 deg); target card shows PGDA AVGVISIB illumination %
layers.mars: Analytic (obliquity 25.19 deg); MCD fluxsurf_dn_sw as cross-check

factors.ui_copy: How high the Sun climbs and how daylight changes through the year. At the Moon's south pole the Sun skims the horizon, casting very long shadows that challenge solar power and camera vision. High-latitude Earth sites get a similar low Sun in summer, though never the airless, black-sky contrast.

factors.name: Atmospheric shielding (radiation + pressure), capped
factors.units: g/cm^2 atmospheric column mass; GV cutoff rigidity (Earth only)

params.earth_score: mean of within-Earth percentiles of (lower column_mass_gcm2) and (lower cutoff_rigidity_gv)
params.cap_rule: ratio similarity of Earth's minimum land column (~320 g/cm^2, Everest) to the target column (Mars ~17 g/cm^2; Moon floored at 1 g/cm^2)

layers.earth: Column mass from elevation (barometric, P/g) + IGRF dipole Stormer cutoff 14.9 cos^4(lambda_m) GV
layers.moon: constant 0 (no atmosphere, no global field); 1369 uSv/d [R20] on the gap panel
layers.mars: Hydrostatic column from MOLA window-mean elevation, 610 Pa * exp(-z/11.1 km) / g_mars (MCD v6.2 GCM topography is too coarse: Gale 619 Pa vs REMS ~850 Pa); checked against MSL RAD 0.64 mSv/d at Gale [R31]

factors.ui_copy: How much air and magnetic field sit overhead to block cosmic radiation. The Moon has neither, and Mars has very thin air. Their surfaces receive roughly 100–200 times the natural radiation dose on Earth, so no Earth site truly matches. This factor only breaks ties between places that already score well, and the real gap appears in the Fidelity Gap panel.

factors.name: Surface UV, capped

params.cap_rule: ratio similarity of Earth's P99.5 UV to the target's Earth-equivalent UV (~10^3 x Earth mean, inferred from [R46])

factors.ui_copy: How strong the Sun's ultraviolet light is at the ground. The Moon gets it unfiltered and Mars gets far more than Earth because its thin air has almost no ozone. High, dry Earth sites get closer but never match, so this factor only breaks ties.

factors.name: Geomorphic flags

layers.earth: Complete catalogues, no hand-picking: impact structures (PASSC Earth Impact Database), Holocene volcanoes (Smithsonian GVP), periglacial = CCI permafrost >= 0.1, massif = land relief >= area-weighted P90; no Earth source for caves, debris-covered glaciers, cold traps
layers.moon: craters, PSRs, massifs from target context
layers.mars: craters, MGC3 caves, debris-covered glaciers, periglacial terrain

factors.ui_copy: Whether the site has telltale landforms shared with the target: impact craters, lava tubes and caves, or frozen-ground patterns. These features let crews rehearse specific tasks, such as exploring a cave or sampling crater rocks, and the challenge names caves explicitly.

layers.earth: MAP travel time to the nearest city of 50k+ (Nelson et al. 2019, 2015 baseline; CC BY 4.0, verify) + Natural Earth airports (public domain, card only)

logistics.easiest_to_reach_rule: hard filter on the candidate pool before set cover: travel_time_min <= 360 (6 h); no cost weighting
logistics.display: site card access line from travel_time_min ('< 1 h', '~{h} h' up to 48 h, then '~{d} days', '> 2 days')

lithology_similarity.note: Provisional matrix (symmetric). Owner: Researcher; finalize before first scoring run.

aggregation.core: S_core = prod(max(s_i, floor) ^ (w_i / sum(w))) over F1-F10 with w_i > 0
aggregation.earth_clip: t* = clip(t, Earth P0.5, Earth P99.5) over land cells (cos(lat) area-weighted quantiles); gap = |t - t*|
aggregation.percentiles: directional percentiles (F7, F11, F12) are cos(lat) area-weighted ranks among land cells

ui_label_source: design/spec.md §7 'UI name' column; factors.json ui_label is the single label source for the UI
